headline: A federal law that expands anti-trafficking training, grants, data reporting, and coordination, and creates a temporary advisory council to address human trafficking.
what_it_does: The law funds and reauthorizes several anti-trafficking grant programs through fiscal years 2021 and 2022, and lets Justice Department grant applicants who support law enforcement get priority. It requires new training for federal employees and tribal officers on spotting and responding to trafficking, and directs agencies to produce reports on trafficking data and investigations. It also changes the definition of a missing child and broadens Secret Service help to state and local police, and it sets up a Public-Private Partnership Advisory Council that ends on September 30, 2020.

who_it_affects.how: They may receive services through reauthorized grant programs, and some victim-service grant recipients must share tools for identifying victims and screening youth.
Federal hiring grants for them can now also pay for training to recognize and respond to signs of human trafficking.

who_it_affects.group: Parents, guardians, and grandparents raising children
who_it_affects.how: The law's definition of a parent now includes legal guardians and people who act as a parent, which affects how a missing child report is handled under the Missing Children's Assistance Act.

who_it_affects.group: Federal, tribal, and state or local law enforcement officers
who_it_affects.how: They may receive advanced anti-trafficking training, technical help on victim-centered investigations, and Secret Service forensic support for any investigation.

who_it_affects.group: Grant applicants for trafficking victim services
who_it_affects.how: Applicants who use funds to prevent, investigate, and prosecute trafficking and who provide long-term resources to police may get priority.
Grant programs now give priority to efforts that improve how courts respond to children who are vulnerable to trafficking.

who_it_affects.group: Members of the public who want to see federal reports
who_it_affects.how: Certain annual reports on missing children and attempted child abductions must be made publicly available.

when_it_takes_effect: Signed into law on December 21, 2018; many provisions set deadlines or funding periods through fiscal years 2021 and 2022, and the advisory council ends on September 30, 2020.
